questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I prioritized convenient and social housing opportunities highly. I didn't want to live in a very big city, and I wanted to a place where you could also get a lot of experiences outside of university life.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I enjoyed my stay very much. The social, cultural and personal aspects of my trip was great. The only downside was the very limited selection of courses relating to my study (physics), and the academic side of my trip suffered a little from this fact.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. The entire university is located at one central campus, and there are a multiple 'help hubs' where you can ask all sorts of questions and get help with all the administration. The university also hosts a lot of events during the introductory week for new international students, so you feel both welcomed and pretty well informed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Introductory events hosted by the university, and the entire housing was organized by university's housing organ (called UniFlats)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There is a housing organ called UniFlats associated with the university. They own a lot of houses throughout the city, almost all of them very close to campus, which they rent out to mainly international students who apply. In most of the houses they also have one Kiwi (New Zealand person) living and they sort of act as the local person that can welcome you, show you around and teach you a bit about the culture.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a fully stocked kitchen. Not prime facilities but they worked fine for me – I only ended up buying a sharper kitchen knife and a french press, everything else was in the kitchen, so totally fine for your regular everyday cooking. The local student association provides a cheap lunch (under 20 DKK) which I made use of often, since it was also quite social. I mostly ate breakfast and dinner in the house.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I highly recommend living with UniFlats! The housing conditions vary a bit in quality – my house was nothing fancy but it was alright. The best thing about it is the social aspect. You get to meet some other international students right away (I lived with three other international students and one kiwi), and I ended up becoming very good friends with two of them. UniFlats also arranges a lot of social events (quiz nights, free lunches, trips to local places etc) which I think are really valuable to international students who doesn't have a big social network.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Also, the rooms are all furnished and they even provide bedding and such. So a very convenient and social way to live, I found that it was a very good decision being away for only one semester.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You get an account on their administration platform (eVision) and apply through there.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was one online seminar that talked about the registration process. For specific course advice, I believe you would have to email the relevant faculty. I got some advice for choosing one of my courses through email.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the classes I wanted, and it was my impression that that was the case for everyone I spoke to.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't worry if everything is not completely in place before you leave. You still have time to change your courses once you are at the uni, and it might be easier to get advice once you are there. I ended up swapping one of my courses for another one into the first week of classes, and it worked out fine.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found that the academic level was lower than what I was used to at KU. In some ways it was okay, since there was a lot of other experiences I was hoping to get while on exchange, and that meant that I had better time to pursue those.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had one 100, one 200 and one 300-level paper – corresponding to first, second and third year papers, respectively. You could tell that the courses was meant for someone early in their university life.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Too many powerpoint shows that were just shot off without intention. The lectures were generally shorter (only 50 minutes) and usually felt quite rushed.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Introduction to Marine Biology (MARI112), Electronics for the Sciences (PHSI245), Experimental Physics II (PHSI381)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The content of Electronics for the Sciences was interesting. It was a quite small class (only 5 people), though, and that dragged it down a bit. The Marine Science paper was interesting for someone with no biology background – very much overview level, though, nothing in depth or heavy substance, but it was interesting and there was a few field trips which meant that I got out the classroom a bit, which was nice.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing too bad. You often want to go on weekend trips (Dunedin not being a very big city) and that does come with some costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is quite expensive in the grocery stores. Drinking coffee out on cafés were quite cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Lots of options through different student clubs and societies.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many different student hosted clubs for all kinds of stuff – check it out clubs on the otago OUSA website.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was a part of the tramping club (OUTC), which hosted some weekend trips and a weekly morning swim, which I became quite fond of. The sauna at OUSA is top notch and a nice place to a small chat to some locals.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: All the lovely nature on the south island (and north island), which is very accessible from Dunedin with a car. There are lots of amazing hikes nearby. Go roadtrip around New Zealand. Take your bike for a ride down Signal Hill. You will find lots of things to do, even though the city is quite small

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. People are more friendly and outgoing in public than what we are used to in Denmark, but they have very much the same down-to-earth atmosphere, and maybe even a bit of Jantelov engrained in them.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Maybe joining the clubs is one of the better ways to do it. I met some friendly local students, but the people I became good friends with were all internationals.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really. Maybe that there is a person hired in the supermarked only to pack your groceries, so where you are used to stressing around in REMA 1000 trying to pack up everything, you just end up standing and staring awkwardly while you wait. But for real, people are friendly and easy to strike up conversations with, and since you also speak their language, you feel somewhat at home pretty quickly.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Learning about the Maori culture (original people of New Zealand) was really cool!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: (1) Live with UniFlats (2) Go to the OUSA sauna at least once (preferably thrice a week) (3) Have fun and  make use of the opportunities that present themselves along the way

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The personal experiences and friendships. Academically, it was probably just improving my oral english

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I did feel a bit of home sickness every now then,

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
